prompt: A PaO2 of 55 mm Hg on room air most closely indicates

options.text: Hypoxemia
Hyperoxia
Normal oxygenation for a healthy young adult
Metabolic alkalosis

explanation: PaO2 below ~60 mm Hg reflects clinically important hypoxemia; normal room-air PaO2 is roughly 80–100 mm Hg.

distractorExplanations.b: Hyperoxia is elevated oxygen tension.
distractorExplanations.c: 55 mm Hg is below normal adult PaO2.
distractorExplanations.d: PaO2 alone does not define metabolic alkalosis.

prompt: An elevated PaCO2 with acidemia is consistent with:

options.text: Respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis (acute or chronic depending on HCO3− compensation)
Metabolic alkalosis as the primary process
Normal acid–base balance

explanation: CO2 retention lowers pH (respiratory acidosis); metabolic compensation raises HCO3− over time.

distractorExplanations.a: Low PaCO2 causes respiratory alkalosis.
distractorExplanations.c: Primary metabolic alkalosis raises HCO3−/pH patterns differently.
distractorExplanations.d: Acidemia with high CO2 is not normal.

prompt: The A-a oxygen gradient widens with:

options.text: Perfect matching of ventilation and perfusion
Breathing room air at sea level with normal lungs
V/Q mismatch, shunt, or diffusion limitation
Hyperventilation in normal lungs exclusively decreasing A-a

explanation: Widened A-aDO2 suggests pulmonary gas-exchange inefficiency rather than pure hypoventilation.

distractorExplanations.a: Ideal V/Q keeps A-a relatively normal.
distractorExplanations.b: Normal lungs have a small A-a gradient.
distractorExplanations.d: Hyperventilation alone does not create a large A-a like shunt does.

prompt: A sudden drop in SpO2 with unilateral absence of breath sounds after central line placement suggests

options.text: Possible right mainstem intubation—pull the tube back 2 cm
Possible pleural effusion—schedule a chest X-ray for the morning
Possible pulmonary embolism—start a heparin drip right away
Possible pneumothorax—assess and notify the team urgently

explanation: Iatrogenic pneumothorax can follow subclavian/internal jugular attempts; asymmetric exam is a red flag.

distractorExplanations.a: Mainstem intubation follows tube placement; a sudden unilateral loss after a central line points to an iatrogenic pneumothorax.
distractorExplanations.b: Effusion develops gradually with dull, diminished sounds; a sudden post-line desaturation needs urgent action, not a morning film.
distractorExplanations.c: PE usually leaves breath sounds present; unilateral absent sounds right after line placement point to pneumothorax.

prompt: Peak inspiratory pressure (PIP) rising with unchanged tidal volume may indicate

options.text: Decreased compliance or increased airway resistance
Increased compliance from improving lung recruitment
A leak in the circuit or around the ETT cuff
Auto-triggering from an overly sensitive trigger setting

explanation: Higher pressure for the same volume means the respiratory system is stiffer or more resistive.

distractorExplanations.b: Higher compliance lowers the pressure needed for the same tidal volume, so PIP would fall, not rise.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaks lower circuit pressures and trigger low-pressure or low-volume alarms rather than a rising PIP.
distractorExplanations.d: Auto-triggering raises the breath rate; it does not raise the peak pressure of each breath at the same tidal volume.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2).

prompt: Plateau pressure (Pplat) best reflects

options.text: Airway resistance, measured as the pressure at peak inspiratory flow
Alveolar pressure related to tidal volume and respiratory system compliance
Intrinsic PEEP, measured with an end-expiratory hold maneuver
Transpulmonary pressure, measured with an esophageal balloon catheter

explanation: Inspiratory hold (zero flow) yields Pplat used for compliance and lung-protective limits. It is measured during an inspiratory hold with no flow.

distractorExplanations.a: Resistance is reflected by PIP minus Pplat; Pplat is taken during a no-flow inspiratory hold and reflects alveolar pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: Auto-PEEP is measured with an expiratory hold; plateau pressure uses an end-inspiratory hold.
distractorExplanations.d: Pplat reflects the whole respiratory system; transpulmonary pressure needs esophageal pressure to subtract the chest wall.

prompt: A patient with suspected CO poisoning may show

options.text: A low PaO2 on the ABG that confirms the degree of CO poisoning
A low SpO2 reading, because pulse oximeters detect COHb as deoxyhemoglobin
Normal or high SpO2 readings that do not reflect true oxygen content
Cyanosis that worsens in proportion to the measured COHb level

explanation: Standard SpO2 cannot reliably distinguish oxyhemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin; CO-oximetry measures COHb. Use CO-oximetry to measure COHb.

distractorExplanations.a: PaO2 reflects dissolved oxygen and is often normal in CO poisoning; it does not measure COHb.
distractorExplanations.b: Standard two-wavelength oximeters read COHb as oxyhemoglobin, giving a falsely normal or high SpO2, not a low one.
distractorExplanations.d: COHb does not cause cyanosis in proportion to its level; cyanosis is an unreliable sign in CO poisoning.

prompt: Dull percussion and bronchial breath sounds over a lung region suggest

options.text: Pneumothorax, which causes dull percussion over the area
Pleural effusion, which causes bronchial breath sounds
Emphysema, which causes dull percussion and bronchial sounds
Consolidation (e.g., pneumonia) more than pneumothorax

explanation: Consolidation increases transmission of bronchial sounds and dulls percussion; pneumothorax is hyperresonant with decreased sounds.

distractorExplanations.a: Pneumothorax gives hyperresonance with absent or diminished breath sounds, not dullness with bronchial sounds.
distractorExplanations.b: Effusion is dull to percussion but breath sounds are diminished or absent over the fluid, not bronchial.
distractorExplanations.c: Emphysema causes hyperresonance and diminished breath sounds from air trapping, not consolidation findings.

prompt: An SBT readiness screen commonly includes:

options.text: Adequate oxygenation, hemodynamic stability, and resolution of the indication for ventilation
Adequate oxygenation on FiO2 0.60 with PEEP 12 cm H2O, plus a stable heart rate and blood pressure
A rapid shallow breathing index above 105 with stable blood pressure
Stable hemodynamics on escalating vasopressors and an improving chest X-ray

explanation: Liberation readiness requires gas exchange and clinical stability sufficient to trial spontaneous breathing. These are screened conceptually before the trial.

distractorExplanations.b: Readiness screens usually require FiO2 of about 0.40-0.50 or less and PEEP of about 5-8 cm H2O, not 0.60 and 12.
distractorExplanations.c: An RSBI below 105 predicts weaning success; a value above 105 predicts failure.
distractorExplanations.d: Escalating vasopressor doses mean the patient is not hemodynamically stable enough for a breathing trial.

Increased TLC in pure restriction
Normal volumes with no change ever

explanation: Restriction lowers volumes; the FEV1/FVC ratio is preserved/elevated, unlike obstruction.

distractorExplanations.a: Low FEV1/FVC defines obstruction.
distractorExplanations.c: Restriction lowers TLC.
distractorExplanations.d: Restriction changes volumes.

prompt: Pedal edema, elevated JVP, and loud P2 in a COPD patient suggest possible

options.text: Left ventricular failure with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema
Tension pneumothorax compressing the great veins
Cor pulmonale / pulmonary hypertension complications
Superior vena cava syndrome from a lung tumor

explanation: Chronic lung disease can cause pulmonary hypertension and right-heart strain with systemic congestion signs.

distractorExplanations.a: LV failure presents with crackles and orthopnea; JVD, pedal edema, and a loud P2 in COPD point to right heart strain.
distractorExplanations.b: Tension pneumothorax is acute with absent breath sounds and tracheal shift, not chronic edema with a loud P2.
distractorExplanations.d: SVC syndrome causes facial and arm swelling with upper-body vein distension, not pedal edema with a loud P2.

prompt: Capnography showing a sudden drop of ETCO2 to near zero may indicate

options.text: Gradual hypoventilation from oversedation, a lower set rate, or progressive respiratory muscle fatigue
Hyperventilation from pain, anxiety, or an increased set rate on the ventilator
Rebreathing from an exhausted CO2 absorber or a faulty expiratory valve in the circuit
Circuit disconnection, esophageal intubation, or catastrophic drop in pulmonary blood flow

explanation: Abrupt ETCO2 loss is an emergency signal for airway/circuit failure or circulatory collapse.

distractorExplanations.a: Hypoventilation raises ETCO2 gradually; a sudden drop to near zero means exhaled CO2 is no longer reaching the sensor.
distractorExplanations.b: Hyperventilation lowers ETCO2 gradually over minutes; it does not drop it abruptly to near zero.
distractorExplanations.c: Rebreathing raises the inspired CO2 baseline above zero; it does not cause a sudden fall to near zero.

prompt: Hemodynamic data: low CVP, low PCWP, and low cardiac output suggest

options.text: Hypovolemia
Fluid overload with high filling pressures
Left ventricular failure with high PCWP
Normal euvolemia with high output

explanation: Low filling pressures with low output fit volume depletion; LV failure typically elevates PCWP.

distractorExplanations.b: Overload raises filling pressures.
distractorExplanations.c: LV failure → high PCWP.
distractorExplanations.d: Low output is not high-output euvolemia.

prompt: A patient with Guillain-Barré is monitored with vital capacity (VC) and NIF because

options.text: Rising VC/NIF values signal the onset of respiratory muscle weakness
Declining VC/NIF can signal impending ventilatory failure
These tests detect hypoxemia earlier than pulse oximetry does
Intubation is indicated once VC falls below 40 mL/kg

explanation: Neuromuscular weakness progresses to hypoventilation; serial respiratory muscle metrics guide ICU timing.

distractorExplanations.a: Weakness lowers VC and makes NIF less negative; rising values mean improving strength.
distractorExplanations.c: VC and NIF measure respiratory muscle strength; hypoxemia is a late sign in neuromuscular failure.
distractorExplanations.d: The usual warning threshold is a VC of about 15-20 mL/kg; 40 mL/kg is still well above the danger zone.

prompt: Methemoglobin clinically may present with:

options.text: Cherry-red skin with a falsely normal SpO2 near 100 percent
Low PaO2 on the ABG that rises once supplemental O2 is added
Cyanosis and chocolate-brown blood with SpO2/PaO2 discrepancies
Pink skin and normal SpO2, since MetHb carries oxygen normally

explanation: MetHb impairs oxygen delivery; methylene blue may be used clinically—diagnosis needs CO-oximetry. Confirm with CO-oximetry.

distractorExplanations.a: That classic (if unreliable) picture belongs to CO poisoning; methemoglobinemia gives cyanosis and SpO2 near 85 percent.
distractorExplanations.b: PaO2 is usually normal in methemoglobinemia; the defect is hemoglobin's inability to carry oxygen.
distractorExplanations.d: Methemoglobin's ferric iron cannot bind oxygen and shifts the curve left, so content and delivery fall.

prompt: A nebulizer that sputters and delivers little aerosol most likely needs

options.text: Checking solution volume, connections, gas flow, and for clogs
Increasing the flow to 15 L/min to force out more aerosol
Adding more saline diluent until the treatment lasts 30 minutes
Replacing the medication with an MDI because the drug has degraded

explanation: Aerosol output depends on adequate volume, intact circuitry, and proper driving flow.

distractorExplanations.b: Running far above the specified 6-8 L/min increases aerosol loss and does not fix a clog, leak, or empty cup.
distractorExplanations.c: Sputtering often means the cup is near empty or faulty; stretching the treatment with diluent does not fix it.
distractorExplanations.d: Drug degradation does not make a nebulizer sputter; the cause is volume, connections, gas flow, or a clog.

prompt: Oxygen blender failure to a set FiO2 should prompt

options.text: Recalibrating the pulse oximeter, since the SpO2 reading is drifting
Verification with an oxygen analyzer and troubleshooting gas supplies/blender
Raising the set FiO2 dial until the patient's SpO2 returns to the ordered target range
Replacing the flowmeter, since blenders cannot fail once calibrated

explanation: Analyzers confirm delivered FiO2; air/O2 supply pressures affect blender output.

distractorExplanations.a: A pulse oximeter measures patient saturation, not delivered FiO2; the blender output needs an oxygen analyzer.
distractorExplanations.c: Compensating with the dial masks a failing blender; delivered FiO2 must be verified with an analyzer.
distractorExplanations.d: Blenders can fail, for example from unequal source-gas pressures; the flowmeter is not the usual culprit.

prompt: A galvanic fuel-cell O2 analyzer reads inaccurately if

options.text: It is calibrated to 21% and 100% oxygen before each use as directed
The battery is low, since galvanic cells need battery power to sense
The fuel cell is depleted or the device is not calibrated to known gases
It is used on dry gas rather than in a humidified circuit

explanation: Fuel cells age; calibration to known O2 concentrations maintains accuracy.

distractorExplanations.a: Two-point calibration against known gases is what keeps the analyzer accurate; it is not a cause of error.
distractorExplanations.b: Galvanic fuel cells generate their own current; batteries are needed by polarographic analyzers, not galvanic ones.
distractorExplanations.d: Dry gas does not cause error; condensed water on the sensor membrane is what degrades accuracy.

prompt: Heated wire circuits on ventilators primarily help

options.text: Warm gas enough to replace the heated humidifier
Filter bacteria from the expiratory gas
Cool the gas so more water condenses in the trap
Reduce condensate in the inspiratory limb

explanation: Heated wires limit rainout while delivering warm humidified gas to artificial airways. They also keep the humidified gas at the set temperature.

distractorExplanations.a: Heated wires only prevent rainout in the tubing; humidity still has to come from the humidifier chamber.
distractorExplanations.b: Expiratory filters capture bacteria; heated wires manage gas temperature and condensation.
distractorExplanations.c: Heated wires do the opposite: they keep the gas warm so less water condenses in the circuit.

options.text: Leak or disconnection in the patient circuit
Patient biting the tube causing high pressure
Kinked ET tube causing high pressure
Improved seal with zero leaks

distractorExplanations.c: Kinks → high pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: Zero leaks would not trigger low-pressure alarms.

prompt: High-pressure ventilator alarms may be caused by:

options.text: Circuit disconnection, a cuff leak, or a loose humidifier chamber
Coughing, secretions, biting, bronchospasm, or decreased compliance
Increased compliance after diuresis or successful recruitment
A low set tidal volume combined with a low inspiratory flow

explanation: Anything raising impedance to inflation can trigger high-pressure limits.

distractorExplanations.a: Disconnections and leaks drop circuit pressure and trigger low-pressure or low-volume alarms instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Higher compliance lowers the pressure needed per breath, which makes high-pressure alarms less likely.
distractorExplanations.d: Lower tidal volume and flow reduce peak pressure; they do not trigger a high-pressure alarm.

prompt: Capnograph calibration/quality issues include

options.text: Sensor drift that requires recalibration against pulse oximetry readings
Colorimetric detectors turning yellow when exposed to room air
Sensor contamination, loose connections, and need for periodic zero/span checks
Reading higher than PaCO2 in healthy lungs, which signals a fault

explanation: ETCO2 devices require maintenance; waveform interpretation depends on valid sensors. Follow the device's instructions.

distractorExplanations.a: Capnographs are zeroed to room air and span-checked with known CO2 gas; pulse oximetry measures oxygenation.
distractorExplanations.b: Colorimetric detectors stay purple in room air and turn yellow when exhaled CO2 is present.
distractorExplanations.d: In healthy lungs ETCO2 normally runs a few mm Hg below PaCO2, so a reading above PaCO2 is not the expected norm.

prompt: A pulse oximeter probe reading poorly on a cold, vasoconstricted finger may improve by:

options.text: Clamping the probe harder until pain guarantees accuracy
Trusting a flat SpO2 of 50% without clinical correlation
Painting nails with opaque polish and ignoring artifacts
Warming the site or using an alternate site/probe designed for low perfusion

explanation: Perfusion and probe placement affect SpO2 accuracy; correlate with clinical picture/ABG when needed.

distractorExplanations.a: Painful clamping is inappropriate.
distractorExplanations.b: Implausible values need verification.
distractorExplanations.c: Polish can artifactually affect readings.

prompt: Autoclaving or improper chemical exposure of reusable devices can

options.text: Damage equipment—follow manufacturer sterilization IFUs
Sterilize the device, so precleaning of soil can be skipped
Be offset by doubling the exposure time for heat-sensitive plastics
Only affect metal parts, since plastics tolerate any autoclave cycle

explanation: IFUs specify compatible disinfection/sterilization; soil must be cleaned before sterilization.

distractorExplanations.b: Cleaning must come before sterilization; residual soil shields microbes and damages surfaces.
distractorExplanations.c: Longer heat or chemical exposure worsens damage to heat-sensitive materials; follow the manufacturer's IFU.

prompt: An oxygen concentrator that fails to reach specified O2 purity should be

options.text: Kept in use with the flow raised to make up for the lower purity
Removed from service and repaired/replaced; verify with analyzer
Kept in use if the purity alarm resets after a restart
Kept in use if purity stays above 70 percent at the prescribed flow

explanation: Substandard purity endangers patients relying on home/long-term O2 systems.

distractorExplanations.a: Raising concentrator flow lowers oxygen purity further; the unit must come out of service.
distractorExplanations.c: A reset alarm does not prove purity; output must be verified with an analyzer and the unit repaired.
distractorExplanations.d: Concentrators should deliver roughly 87-95 percent oxygen at the set flow; 70 percent is far below specification.

prompt: Wright respirometer (or similar) used for VC/VT measurement requires:

options.text: Placing it on the inspiratory side of the circuit so it measures the delivered volume
Connecting it to a high-flow oxygen source to drive the vane properly
Proper assembly, leak-free connections, and correct patient technique coaching
Calibration against a peak flowmeter before each patient measurement

explanation: Volume devices need intact circuitry and coached efforts for valid spirometric bedside measures.

distractorExplanations.a: Wright-type respirometers measure exhaled volume; placement on the expiratory side is standard.
distractorExplanations.b: The patient's exhaled gas drives the vane; no external gas source is connected.
distractorExplanations.d: Volume accuracy is checked with a calibrated syringe, not by comparison with a peak flowmeter.

prompt: Heliox delivery systems require attention to:

options.text: Using air flowmeters, which read high, so delivered flow is lower
Choosing heliox mainly for its higher density to slow airflow
Using a 70/30 mix for hypoxemic patients who need FiO2 above 0.50
Correct gas mixture and appropriately calibrated flow devices

explanation: Low-density heliox alters flowmeter behavior and may affect some nebulizers/ventilators. Airway and device compatibility also matter.

distractorExplanations.b: Helium's benefit is its low density, which reduces turbulent flow resistance, not a higher density.
distractorExplanations.c: A 70/30 mix supplies FiO2 0.30; patients needing much more oxygen lose most of the helium benefit.

Charge status only, since vacuum level is fixed by the factory
Canister size and the date of the last biomedical inspection
Wall vacuum connection, since portable units run on wall suction

prompt: Quality control for blood gas analyzers includes:

prompt: Indications for oxygen therapy include

options.text: Documented hypoxemia or clinical conditions with high risk of hypoxemia
Dyspnea in any patient, even when SpO2 and PaO2 are normal on room air at rest
SpO2 below 96 percent in adults with no other risk factors
Hypercapnia, since oxygen lowers PaCO2 in ventilatory failure

Moderate FiO2 that varies with fit and flow
FiO2 near 0.90 when run at 10–15 L/min
Room-air FiO2 when the flow is set at 5 L/min

Encourage sustained maximal inspiration to prevent/treat atelectasis
Strengthen expiratory muscles through repeated resisted exhalations

Delivering positive pressure on inspiration like intermittent positive pressure breathing

prompt: Recruitment maneuvers and high PEEP strategies require caution because they may cause

options.text: Hypotension and barotrauma in susceptible patients
Hypertension from increased venous return to the heart
Bradycardia and pulmonary edema from lowered pleural pressure
Increased cardiac output from improved oxygenation

explanation: Increased intrathoracic pressure can reduce venous return; overdistension risks pneumothorax.

distractorExplanations.b: Raised intrathoracic pressure decreases venous return, which causes hypotension rather than hypertension.
distractorExplanations.c: Recruitment and high PEEP raise pleural pressure; the main risks are hypotension and barotrauma.
distractorExplanations.d: High intrathoracic pressure usually lowers cardiac output by reducing preload.

prompt: Prone positioning in severe ARDS is used to:

options.text: Lower plateau pressure enough to allow higher tidal volumes
Improve oxygenation by redistributing perfusion/ventilation
Improve secretion drainage as the primary goal of the therapy
Reduce the need for sedation during mechanical ventilation

explanation: Proning can improve V/Q in severe ARDS; teams manage lines, airway, and pressure points. This works in many patients.

distractorExplanations.a: Proning is used with low tidal volumes; it is not a way to justify larger tidal volumes.
distractorExplanations.c: Secretion drainage is a side benefit; prone positioning is used mainly to improve oxygenation.
distractorExplanations.d: Prone positioning often requires deep sedation and sometimes paralysis, not less sedation.

prompt: Aerosolized medication delivery during mechanical ventilation is improved by:

options.text: Placing the nebulizer at the Y-piece with bias flow running at its highest setting
Leaving the HME in place between the nebulizer and the patient
Optimal nebulizer/MDI adapter placement, synchronizing when appropriate
Increasing humidification to maximum, since humid gas boosts particle delivery

explanation: Device position and ventilator interactions affect inhaled dose; follow evidence-based aerosol practices. Minimizing circuit losses per best practice also helps.

distractorExplanations.a: High bias flow washes aerosol into the expiratory limb; bias flow is reduced during nebulization.
distractorExplanations.b: An HME traps aerosol particles; it must be removed or bypassed during in-line aerosol delivery.
distractorExplanations.d: Humidified gas enlarges particles and lowers deposition; humidity reduces, not boosts, delivery.

prompt: Chest physiotherapy (postural drainage/percussion) is relatively contraindicated in:

options.text: Cystic fibrosis with thick secretions and frequent exacerbations
Lobar atelectasis caused by mucus plugging after surgery
Bronchiectasis with daily sputum production over 30 mL
Active hemoptysis, unstable spinal injury, or untreated pneumothorax

explanation: External maneuvers can worsen bleeding, fractures, or air leaks—screen contraindications. These are classic cautions.

distractorExplanations.a: Cystic fibrosis with retained secretions is a core indication for chest physiotherapy, not a contraindication.
distractorExplanations.b: Atelectasis from mucus plugging is an indication for postural drainage and percussion.
distractorExplanations.c: Sputum production over about 25-30 mL per day is an indication for chest physiotherapy.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2).

prompt: The primary goal of bronchial hygiene therapy is to:

options.text: Assist removal of retained secretions and improve ventilation/perfusion
Reverse bronchospasm by relaxing airway smooth muscle directly with each treatment
Prevent atelectasis by sustained maximal inspiration alone
Reduce airway inflammation and mucus production over time

explanation: Clearance therapies target mucus plugging/retention—not structural fibrosis cure or unsafe ICP rises. This matters where secretions impair gas exchange.

distractorExplanations.b: Relaxing airway smooth muscle is the goal of bronchodilators, not bronchial hygiene therapy.
distractorExplanations.c: Sustained maximal inspiration is lung expansion therapy such as incentive spirometry.
distractorExplanations.d: Reducing inflammation is the role of inhaled corticosteroids; bronchial hygiene removes secretions.

prompt: When titrating O2 in a patient at risk for hypercapnic respiratory failure, best practice is to?

options.text: Target SpO2 of 94–98 percent, as for most other adult patients
Target appropriate SpO2 goals and monitor ventilation/ABG
Avoid oxygen until an ABG confirms the PaCO2 level
Use a nonrebreather to keep SpO2 at 100 percent

explanation: Titrate to goals (often ~88–92% in at-risk COPD per many protocols) while watching for CO2 retention/clinical decline. Monitor as clinically indicated.

distractorExplanations.a: The 94-98 percent target applies to most adults; patients at risk of hypercapnic failure usually get a lower 88-92 percent target.
distractorExplanations.c: Oxygen should not be withheld from a hypoxemic patient while waiting for an ABG.
distractorExplanations.d: Hyperoxia in these patients can worsen hypercapnia; oxygen is titrated to a target range.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2).

prompt: Intrapulmonary percussive ventilation (IPV) / high-frequency chest wall devices are used to:

options.text: Measure airway resistance before and after bronchodilator use
Strengthen inspiratory muscles before ventilator weaning
Mobilize secretions as part of an airway clearance program
Replace the need for patient coughing to clear secretions

explanation: High-frequency devices are clearance adjuncts selected by clinical protocol and tolerance.

distractorExplanations.a: Bronchodilator response is measured with pulmonary function testing, not airway clearance devices.
distractorExplanations.b: Building inspiratory strength is inspiratory muscle training, not IPV or chest wall oscillation.
distractorExplanations.d: These devices loosen secretions, but coughing or suctioning is still needed to remove them.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2).

prompt: The first action for an unresponsive, apneic patient is to:

options.text: Activate emergency response and begin CAB/ABCs
Check a carotid pulse for a full 30 seconds
Give two rescue breaths before calling for help
Apply oxygen by nonrebreather and recheck in 1 minute

explanation: Basic life support priorities precede advanced diagnostics in arrest/near-arrest. Open the airway and provide ventilation or CPR as indicated.

distractorExplanations.b: Pulse checks are limited to 10 seconds or less so compressions are not delayed.
distractorExplanations.c: For an unresponsive adult, help is activated first and adult CPR follows the CAB sequence.
distractorExplanations.d: An apneic patient needs ventilation and CPR as indicated; passive oxygen does nothing without breathing.

prompt: Suspected tension pneumothorax with hypotension and tracheal deviation needs

options.text: A chest X-ray to confirm before any intervention
Immediate decompression per emergency protocol
Increasing PEEP to re-expand the collapsed lung
A 12-lead ECG to rule out cardiac tamponade

explanation: Tension physiology is immediately life-threatening; decompression is the priority. Support oxygenation and ventilation.

distractorExplanations.a: Tension pneumothorax with hypotension is a clinical diagnosis; waiting for imaging delays lifesaving decompression.
distractorExplanations.c: Added positive pressure enlarges a tension pneumothorax and worsens hypotension.
distractorExplanations.d: Tracheal deviation with hypotension points to tension pneumothorax; an ECG delays decompression.

prompt: Foreign-body airway obstruction with severe signs in a conscious adult is treated with:

options.text: Back blows only, since thrusts injure adult patients
Encouraging forceful coughing until the object clears
Abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) or approved protocol
A blind finger sweep followed by rescue breaths

explanation: Severe FBAO needs immediate dislodgement maneuvers per BLS guidelines. Continue until expulsion or the patient becomes unresponsive.

distractorExplanations.a: Abdominal thrusts are the recommended adult response for severe obstruction despite injury risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Coughing is encouraged in mild obstruction; severe signs (cannot speak or cough) need thrusts.
distractorExplanations.d: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper and are not recommended.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2).

prompt: During cardiac arrest, ETCO2 suddenly rises toward normal with ROSC because

options.text: Ventilation rate increases, washing more CO2 out of the lungs
Epinephrine raises CO2 production in the tissues
The ETT has moved from the esophagus into the trachea
Pulmonary blood flow resumes and delivers CO2 to the lungs

explanation: ETCO2 is a surrogate of pulmonary perfusion during CPR; rise suggests ROSC.

distractorExplanations.a: Faster ventilation lowers ETCO2; the abrupt rise at ROSC reflects restored pulmonary perfusion.
distractorExplanations.b: Epinephrine can transiently lower ETCO2; the sudden rise at ROSC comes from restored blood flow.
distractorExplanations.c: An esophageal tube reads near zero throughout; the ROSC rise occurs with a correctly placed tube.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2).

prompt: Accidental extubation with inadequate breathing requires:

options.text: Airway support with BVM and preparation for reintubation as needed
Immediate reintubation without first oxygenating the patient
High-flow nasal cannula at 60 L/min and reassess in an hour
A nonrebreather mask and an ABG before any airway decision

explanation: Re-establish oxygenation/ventilation first; then secure a definitive airway.

distractorExplanations.b: The patient is oxygenated and ventilated with a BVM first; rushing reintubation risks hypoxemia.
distractorExplanations.c: Inadequate breathing needs assisted ventilation; high-flow cannula does not ventilate the patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for an ABG delays needed ventilation; inadequate breathing calls for BVM support now.

prompt: Malignant hyperthermia crisis support includes:

options.text: Switching from sevoflurane to desflurane and continuing the case
Stopping triggering agents and hyperventilating with 100% O2
Reducing minute ventilation to let PaCO2 rise and stimulate breathing
Giving succinylcholine to relieve the muscle rigidity quickly

explanation: MH is a hypermetabolic emergency; anesthesia teams lead dantrolene protocols while RTs support ventilation/cooling logistics. Support dantrolene and protocol care.

distractorExplanations.a: All volatile anesthetics trigger malignant hyperthermia; switching agents does not remove the trigger.
distractorExplanations.c: MH drives CO2 production up; minute ventilation is increased to clear CO2, not reduced.
distractorExplanations.d: Succinylcholine is itself an MH trigger; dantrolene is the treatment for rigidity.

prompt: Status asthmaticus deteriorating on NPPV with exhaustion suggests

options.text: Increasing EPAP to 15 to keep NPPV going
Switching to high-flow nasal cannula
Need for intubation/mechanical ventilation
Adding heliox and continuing NPPV overnight

explanation: Fatigue/hypercapnia despite maximal therapy indicates invasive support; vent strategies allow exhalation. Use a ventilator strategy that avoids air trapping.

distractorExplanations.a: Exhaustion on NPPV signals failure; raising settings and continuing delays needed intubation.
distractorExplanations.b: High-flow cannula gives less ventilatory support than NPPV and cannot rescue an exhausted patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Heliox can bridge some patients, but exhaustion means intubation now rather than continuing overnight.

prompt: Massive hemoptysis initial priorities include

options.text: Positioning the bleeding side up to drain blood out of it
Chest physiotherapy to clear clots from the bleeding lung
Incentive spirometry to keep the bleeding lung expanded
Airway protection (often bleeding side down) and oxygenation

explanation: Protect the airway and non-bleeding lung; control bleeding with specialist care. Then activate urgent team and bronchoscopy pathways.

distractorExplanations.a: Bleeding side up lets blood spill into the good lung; the bleeding side goes down.
distractorExplanations.b: Percussion and drainage are contraindicated in active hemoptysis and can worsen bleeding.
distractorExplanations.c: Lung expansion therapy is not a priority; the airway and oxygenation come first in massive hemoptysis.

prompt: Fire in the OR with an airway fire requires:

options.text: Stop ventilation/gases as protocol directs, remove burning tube, extinguish
Increase FiO2 to 1.0 and keep ventilating through the tube
Leave the tube in place and flush it with saline while continuing to ventilate with oxygen
Stop the laser and continue ventilation with nitrous oxide

explanation: Airway fire algorithms prioritize removing the fuel/oxidizer source and protecting the patient. Then re-establish the airway and oxygenation.

distractorExplanations.b: Oxygen feeds an airway fire; gas flow is stopped and the burning tube removed.
distractorExplanations.c: The burning tube is removed and ventilation stopped; ventilating through it keeps feeding the fire.
distractorExplanations.d: Nitrous oxide supports combustion as strongly as oxygen; all gas flow is stopped.

prompt: Auto-PEEP with progressive hypotension on the ventilator may require

options.text: Increasing the set rate to shorten each breath and reduce trapping
Temporarily disconnecting to allow exhalation / lowering rate and I:E adjustments
Adding applied PEEP well above the measured auto-PEEP level to splint the airways open
Increasing tidal volume and inspiratory time to improve CO2 removal and oxygenation

explanation: Severe air trapping impairs venous return; allow exhalation and adjust settings. Follow protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: A higher rate shortens expiratory time and increases auto-PEEP; the rate is lowered instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Applied PEEP above the intrinsic level adds to hyperinflation and worsens hypotension.
distractorExplanations.d: Larger volumes and longer inspiration leave less time to exhale and increase air trapping.

prompt: Anaphylaxis with respiratory distress is treated urgently with:

options.text: Diphenhydramine IV as the first-line drug, then reassess
Methylprednisolone IV to stop the reaction within minutes
Epinephrine IM (per protocol) and airway/oxygen support
Epinephrine IV push of 1 mg (1:1,000) as the first dose

explanation: IM epinephrine is first-line for anaphylaxis; airway support is concurrent. Activate the emergency response.

distractorExplanations.a: Antihistamines are adjuncts; IM epinephrine is the first-line drug in anaphylaxis.
distractorExplanations.b: Corticosteroids take hours to act and are not first-line; epinephrine is.
distractorExplanations.d: A 1 mg IV bolus is cardiac-arrest dosing; first-line anaphylaxis dosing is about 0.3-0.5 mg IM.

prompt: Post-intubation deterioration with asymmetric chest rise after clavicle line placement suggests

options.text: Bronchospasm, treated first with a bronchodilator nebulizer
Cuff leak, treated by adding air to the ETT pilot balloon
Pulmonary edema from the line's fluid bolus, treated with diuretics
Mainstem intubation or pneumothorax—assess, auscultate, adjust tube depth

explanation: Acute asymmetry after intubation/central lines demands rapid differentiation of tube malposition vs PTX. Image or decompress as indicated.

distractorExplanations.a: Bronchospasm causes bilateral wheeze and high pressures, not asymmetric chest rise.
distractorExplanations.b: A cuff leak causes audible leak and low volumes, not one-sided chest rise.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulmonary edema gives bilateral crackles; asymmetric chest rise points to tube position or pneumothorax.

prompt: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes may need respiratory therapy support for:

options.text: Ventilatory support if arrest/respiratory failure occurs
Albuterol by nebulizer as the definitive way to remove potassium
Hypoventilation to raise PaCO2 and drive potassium into cells
Sodium bicarbonate nebulization to lower serum potassium

explanation: RTs manage airway/ventilation emergencies while medical teams shift/remove potassium. Medical therapy (calcium, shifts) proceeds alongside.

distractorExplanations.b: Albuterol shifts potassium into cells temporarily; it does not remove potassium from the body.
distractorExplanations.c: Respiratory acidosis moves potassium out of cells; alkalosis is what shifts it in.
distractorExplanations.d: Bicarbonate is given IV when used; it is not a nebulized respiratory therapy for hyperkalemia.

prompt: Disaster/mass-casualty oxygen allocation planning emphasizes

options.text: Giving every patient 15 L/min by nonrebreather until supplies run out
Titrating O2 to clinically appropriate targets and conserving resources
Allocating oxygen first-come, first-served as patients arrive
Reserving cylinders for ventilated patients and stopping all others

explanation: Crisis standards still aim for best outcomes with limited O2—assessment and titration matter. Use triage frameworks.

distractorExplanations.a: Untitrated maximal flow exhausts supply quickly; oxygen is titrated to targets in a mass-casualty event.
distractorExplanations.c: Allocation follows triage by need and likely benefit, not arrival order.
distractorExplanations.d: Non-ventilated hypoxemic patients still need titrated oxygen; triage frameworks guide allocation.

prompt: Difficult airway algorithms prioritize

options.text: Repeated direct laryngoscopy attempts until the tube passes, then oxygenating
Proceeding straight to a surgical airway after the first failed laryngoscopy attempt by anyone
Oxygenation first, calling for help, and progressing through established failed-airway pathways
Paralyzing again and trying blind nasal intubation before calling for help

explanation: Cannot-intubate/cannot-oxygenate pathways emphasize oxygen, help, and rescue devices/cricothyrotomy. This includes a surgical airway when needed.

distractorExplanations.a: Attempts are limited and oxygenation is maintained between them; repeated attempts cause airway trauma.
distractorExplanations.b: A surgical airway is for a cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate situation after BVM or supraglottic rescue fails.
distractorExplanations.d: Help is called early; blind nasal attempts are not part of standard failed-airway pathways.
